You already know where the notes are. What's new is that an organ is worked differently:
your hands pick the notes, but your **feet and your left hand's spare moments** make the
music louder, softer, calmer or wilder. This lesson shows you how, first on the organ
on this page and then on the school's **Yamaha MODX+**.

## 1. Five ways an organ is not a piano

1. **No touch.** Hit a key hard or soft: it's the same volume. Don't waste energy
   hammering it.
2. **No decay.** A piano note fades away; an organ note stays at full volume until you
   let go. So *when you let go* matters as much as when you press. Short notes need
   you to lift on purpose.
3. **No sustain pedal.** Holding notes is done with your fingers. Play legato by
   finger-sliding, the way you would for a slow hymn, not with your right foot.
4. **Your right foot plays volume.** It goes on the **swell pedal** (section 4).
5. **You build the sound yourself** with the **drawbars** (section 2), and a spinning
   speaker, the **Leslie**, gives it motion (section 5).

A practical one: because notes don't fade, big piano chords with lots of notes get
muddy fast. Organists often play **three or four notes** in the right hand and keep the
left hand light or leave the bass to someone else.

Try it on the organ below: press **Hold a chord**, then work the controls.

<div class="ar-organ"></div>

## 2. Drawbars: building the sound

There are nine bars. Each one adds a pitch above or below the note you play, from 0
(pushed in, silent) to 8 (pulled all the way out). You write a setting as nine digits in
groups of 2, 4 and 3: **88 8000 000** means the first three are out and the rest are in.
(The organ lesson [Arranging 4: The Organ](arrange-organ.qmd) explains what each bar is.)

You don't need to invent settings. Players have favourites, and these are some that
HammondWiki lists. They're all in the **Start from** menu above, or type or paste any setting into the
**Or type / paste** box.

| Setting | What it's for |
|---|---|
| **88 8000 000** | The standard jazz and blues sound. HammondWiki says the standard jazz settings "will make your organ sound like 90% of the recorded jazz material extant", and lists this one for Jimmy Smith. Start here. |
| **88 8800 000** | Adds the 4′ so it cuts through a band. HammondWiki lists it for the first chorus of "Green Onions". |
| **88 8000 008** | Gospel: the round sound with a whistle on top. |
| **88 8630 000** | HammondWiki's setting for Booker T. Jones. |
| **84 8848 448** and **88 8888 888** | The two HammondWiki gives for Steve Winwood. The second is every bar out. |
| **80 0808 000** | Procol Harum ("A Whiter Shade of Pale"): a hollow, churchy sound. |
| **68 8600 000** | Soft and warm, for a ballad. |

**Rule of thumb:** more bars out, louder and brighter. Fewer, softer and rounder. The
bars on the left give weight. The ones on the right give bite and sparkle.

## 3. Percussion: the "ping"

Many organs have a switch called **percussion**. It adds a short "ping" at the start of
each note, a 2nd or 3rd harmonic that dies away fast. It's the bright, plucky attack you
hear in jazz organ. What HammondWiki says about it:

- It is **single-trigger**: it only pings when you press a key with **all other keys
  up**. If you play legato (holding one note while you press the next), the next note
  doesn't ping. To hear it on every note, play slightly **detached**.
- On a real Hammond it only works on the **upper keyboard**, and it uses up the 1′
  drawbar's contact, so that bar goes silent while percussion is on.
- **"Four Up"** is the classic jazz setting: percussion **On, Soft, Fast, 3rd**. The name
  comes from the four switches on a B-3 all being in the up position.

The organ on this page doesn't model percussion yet. On the MODX+, organ Performances
with "Perc" or "Percussion" in the name have it built in (section 6).

## 4. The swell pedal: your volume

The swell pedal is a volume pedal for your right foot. **Heel down** is quiet. **Toe
down** is full. It never goes completely silent.

When to move it:

- **Into a big moment:** open it gradually over the bar or two before a chorus or a hit,
  so the band arrives with you.
- **After a big hit:** pull it back quickly so the next part has somewhere to grow.
- **On a long chord:** lean into it, the way a singer swells a long note. A held organ
  chord that doesn't move sounds dead. A small swell keeps it alive.
- **Under a singer:** keep it low through the verse. The organ is "furniture" there.
- **Don't pump it on every beat.** That just sounds like someone stepping on a pedal.

## 5. The Leslie: slow and fast

The Leslie is a speaker cabinet with a **spinning horn** (high notes) and a **spinning
drum** (low notes). It has two speeds:

- **Slow (chorale):** a gentle, wide sway. Your default.
- **Fast (tremolo):** a shimmering, urgent swirl. For excitement.

The magic is in the **change**. The horn speeds up in about a second and a half, and the
heavy drum takes several seconds. That "wind-up" is a sound people listen for. So:

- **Switch to fast for a lift:** at the end of a phrase going into a chorus, under a
  solo, at a climax.
- **Switch back to slow when the energy drops:** a new verse, a quiet bridge.
- **A quick flick:** fast for half a bar on a held chord, then straight back to slow.
- **Don't change speed every bar.** Save it, so it means something.

Hold a chord on the organ at the top of the page and switch Slow → Fast → Slow. Listen
for the wind-up and the wind-down.

## 6. Setting up the MODX+

The MODX+ doesn't have drawbars or a swell pedal you can see. You get them through its
organ **Performances**, its controllers and a pedal.

**Before class: plug in a pedal.** The swell pedal is a **Yamaha FC7** foot controller
plugged into the **FOOT CONTROLLER [1]** jack on the back. (A sustain *footswitch* is a
different thing: it only does on/off.)

**Pick an organ sound:**

1. Press **[CATEGORY]**, then choose **Organ**, then **Tone Wheel**. Those are the Hammond-style
   sounds. ("Combo" is the 1960s Vox / Farfisa type. "Pipe" is church organ.)
2. Good ones to start with: **The Basics**, **All 9 Bars!**, **Jazz Organ**, **The
   Preacher**, **Overdriven Organ**. Some Performance names are drawbar settings, for example
   **8.8.8.8.6.2.2.0.0**.

**Find the Leslie switch.** On each Performance a controller is set to change the
rotary speaker's speed. Usually it's **[ASSIGN 1]** / **[ASSIGN 2]** or the **mod wheel**. To check
which one:

1. Press **[EDIT]**, touch **Control**, then **Control Assign**.
2. Look for the Destination **InsA SpdCtrl** or **InsB SpdCtrl** (the rotary speaker's speed). Its
   **Source** is the button or wheel that does it. If there's none, you can add one: set
   Source to **AsgnSw 1** and Destination to **Ins A SpdCtrl** (or B, whichever insert
   effect is the Rotary Speaker).

**Make the pedal the swell.** In the same Control area, the **Control Number** tab sets
which message **Foot Ctrl 1** sends. For a volume pedal, set it to the Expression
controller (**11**) and check the Part responds. If the pedal does nothing to the
volume, it's set to something else. Ask your teacher before saving over a preset.

**Drawbars on the MODX+:** many organ Performances put drawbar-like levels on the
**knobs** or **sliders**. Move them while you hold a chord and listen. Once you have a
sound you like, **[STORE]** it as a new Performance with your name on it, and don't
overwrite the preset.

*Checked against the MODX+ Owner's Manual and Reference Manual: the FC7 and the
FOOT CONTROLLER jacks, Category Search, Control Assign and the Rotary Speaker's
SpdCtrl. **Not checked on the keyboard:** which controller each preset uses for the
Leslie, whether Foot Ctrl 1 defaults to Expression, and what the knobs do on each organ
Performance. Try it and write what you find on the class sheet.*

## 7. Sample lesson: "Gimme Some Lovin'"

"Gimme Some Lovin'" (the Spencer Davis Group, 1966) was a Top 10 single in several
countries. Its organ is played by **Steve Winwood**, who also sings it. It's a good song for
learning the swell pedal and the Leslie, because it goes from riff to verse to chorus
and back. That gives you places to build and places to pull back.

*Which way Winwood moved the pedal and the Leslie on the record isn't written down here
anywhere we've checked. The plan below is a **teaching plan**: what a pianist might do
to make the song's shape clear. Students listen to the record and argue with it.*

**Goal:** you decide where to swell and where to change Leslie speed, and you can say
why.

**1. Listen (10 min).** Play the recording. Students draw the song's shape as a line:
up where it gets more intense, down where it calms. Mark the intro riff, the verses,
the chorus, and the ending.

**2. Set up (5 min).** On the MODX+: a Tone Wheel organ, FC7 in, and the Leslie switch
found (section 6). A full, rock setting: try **88 8888 888** or Winwood's
**84 8848 448** if the Performance lets you set bars. Leslie **slow**.

**3. Map the controls onto the shape (10 min).** Before anyone plays, the class fills
this in. Here is one answer to compare with:

| Part of the song | Swell pedal | Leslie | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intro riff | Open, near full | Slow | The riff has to punch, and slow keeps it clear |
| Verse | Pull back about a third | Slow | Make room for the voice |
| End of verse into the chorus | Open steadily over the last bar or two | **Switch to fast** on the last bar | The wind-up *is* the lift into the chorus |
| Chorus | Full | Fast | Peak energy |
| Back to the riff / next verse | Snap back a little | **Back to slow** at the start of the new section | The wind-down marks "new section" |
| Ending | Full, then let the last chord swell | Fast on the last chord | Big finish |

**4. Play it (15 min).** In pairs: one plays the riff and chords, the other works the
pedal and the Leslie button. Then swap. Finally, one person does all of it. That's the
real skill: your feet and a spare finger working while your hands keep the part going.

**5. Check (5 min).** Record one take. Listen back and ask:

- Can you *hear* the chorus coming before it arrives? (If not: start the swell earlier.)
- Did the Leslie change sound like an event, or like noise? (If noise: you're changing
  it too often.)
- In the verse, could you hear the singer (or imagine one)? (If not: less pedal, fewer
  notes.)

**Extension:** take the same plan to a slow song (try **68 8600 000**, Leslie slow the
whole way, the swell doing all the work). Or try a jazz blues with **88 8000 000** and
"Four Up" percussion, played detached so every note pings.
